summary: This unit teaches you to give a safe, relaxing and effective facial: prepare the room and the client, consult and check for contraindications, cleanse, analyse the skin under the magnifying lamp, and choose products for the skin type. You will learn to exfoliate, steam, massage, apply and remove masks, tone and moisturise, adapt the facial for sensitive skin, deeper skin tones and male clients, deal with contra-actions, give aftercare and home-care advice and keep records.

blocks.p: This unit covers a full facial treatment, from setting up the room to cleaning the steamer and filling in the client's record card. It is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees. A facial cleans the skin deeply, improves its look and feel, relaxes the client, and gives you the chance to advise her on caring for her skin at home.

Done well, a facial leaves the skin clean, fresh and calm. Done badly, it can burn the skin with steam or a hot towel, spread an infection such as a cold sore, trigger an allergy, or leave dark marks on deeper skin tones from rough squeezing. That is why this unit is about **analysis, safety, hygiene and judgement** as much as technique.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and two practical tasks. In one you give a cleanse, tone and moisturise facial with a skin analysis. In the other you plan and give a full facial for a given skin type, with exfoliation, steam (or a warm compress), a massage of about 10 to 15 minutes, and a mask. The assessor watches your consultation, safety, hygiene, method, adaptations and records.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, take close-ups of the work area only, with the client's eyes covered by damp cotton pads. Take a whole-face photo only if the client agrees in writing and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The client lies still with her eyes closed and trusts you with her face. You must keep her warm, safe and comfortable, keep germs from passing between clients, and use electrical equipment, hot water and steam with care.

ul: Clean, quiet and private, with soft lighting and fresh air.
Comfortably warm. A client lying still soon feels cold, especially under air conditioning: have a blanket or towel ready.
Couch wiped with disinfectant and covered with fresh towels and **couch roll** (a disposable paper roll) for every client.
Couch and stool set at heights that let you work with a straight back and relaxed shoulders, feet flat, without twisting.
Trolley wiped with disinfectant and laid out in the order you will work, with a lined, lidded bin close by.

head: Shelf
What goes on it
rows: Top
Products for the client's skin type, in order of use: eye make-up remover, cleanser, toner, exfoliant, massage medium, mask, moisturiser with SPF. Clean spatulas, bowls, mask brush.
Middle
Cotton pads, tissues, sponges or mitts, headband, bowls of warm water, eye pads, gloves.
Bottom
Spare towels, couch roll, a blanket; record card and skin analysis chart.

ul: Wash your hands before and after every client; keep your nails short and clean and your hair tied back.
Fresh towels, couch roll and headband for every client. Used towels go straight into a closed laundry bin.
Take creams out of jars with a **clean spatula**, never your fingers, and close the lid at once. Germs from fingers grow in the jar and reach the next client.
Cotton pads, tissues, disposable spatulas and disposable sponges are used once and go straight into a **lined, lidded bin**.
Reusable sponges and mitts are washed and disinfected as the maker says, or laundered hot; never used on two clients without cleaning.
Bowls and mask brushes are washed, then disinfected for the time the maker gives.
Wear gloves for any extraction or if there is any blood or tissue fluid. A used lancet or blade goes in the **sharps box**.
Store products in a cool, dry place, closed and labelled; use them before the expiry date and within the open-jar time (for example, '12M' means 12 months after opening).

head: Equipment
Check before use
Use it safely
rows: Facial steamer
Cable and plug undamaged
Filled to the line with distilled water (unless the maker says otherwise)
On a stable base, cable tidy
Pre-heat it with the nozzle turned **away** from the client until the steam is steady, not spitting
Cover her eyes with damp cotton pads
Set the distance and time for her skin; never leave her alone with it
Turn it away and switch off before she sits up; empty, clean and descale it as the maker says
Magnifying lamp
Cable, arm and lens undamaged
Lens clean
Cover the client's eyes before you bring the lamp over
Move the arm slowly and keep it clear of her face
Cover the lens when not in use: sunlight through it can focus heat and start a fire
Hot towels and warm compresses
Towel clean; cabinet or water at the right heat
Wring out well; **test on the inside of your wrist** before it touches the face
Leave the nose and mouth uncovered
Ask the client if it is comfortable
All electrical items
No damaged cables or loose plugs
Made for the socket used (110 V or 220 V)
Keep water away from sockets and plugs; dry your hands
Report faulty equipment and do not use it

blocks.note: Tap water in many parts of Jamaica is hard: it carries minerals that build up as scale inside a steamer. Scale can make the steamer spit drops of hot water. That is why most makers say to fill steamers with distilled water and descale them regularly.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: If a steamer starts spitting hot drops, turn the nozzle away from the client at once, switch it off, and check the water level and the water used before you go on. Never fill or empty a steamer while it is switched on or still hot.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Layer
What it is
Why it matters in a facial
rows: Epidermis
The thin outer layer. New cells form at its base and move up to the surface, where they die, flatten and shed. Its base holds the **melanocytes**, the cells that make melanin (skin colour).
Cleansing and exfoliation work here. The skin renews its surface about every 4 weeks in a young adult (more slowly with age), which is why facials are often booked about 4 weeks apart.
Dermis

The thicker layer underneath: collagen and elastin fibres (firmness and stretch), blood vessels, nerves, hair follicles, **sebaceous glands** (which make sebum, the skin's natural oil) and sweat glands.
Massage and steam increase the blood flow here. Loss of collagen and elastin causes lines and sagging.
Subcutaneous layer
Fat beneath the dermis.
Cushions and shapes the face; thins with age.

blocks.p: Healthy skin is slightly acid (about pH 4.5 to 5.5). This **acid mantle**, made of sweat and sebum, helps protect the skin from germs. Harsh soaps and strong products strip it, leaving the skin tight and easily irritated.

head: Skin type
What you see and feel
What it needs
rows: Normal
Neither oily nor dry; smooth, even surface; small pores; few blemishes.
Gentle products that keep it balanced.
Dry (lacks oil)
Fine texture, small pores, flaky patches, feels tight, fine lines show early.
Creamy cleanser, mild alcohol-free toner, richer moisturiser, non-setting mask.
Oily
Shine all over, enlarged (open) pores, blackheads and spots, thicker texture.
Foaming gel or light lotion cleanser, astringent, clay mask, light oil-free moisturiser.
Combination
Oily **T-zone** (forehead, nose and chin) with normal or dry cheeks. The most common type.
Treat each area for what it needs: for example, clay mask on the T-zone, cream mask on the cheeks.
Sensitive
Reddens easily, may sting or itch with products, often fine and thin with broken capillaries.
Mild, fragrance-free products; little heat; light pressure; no tapotement.
Mature
Less firm and elastic; lines and wrinkles; often drier.
Rich, nourishing products; gentle handling; non-setting masks.

head: Condition
What it is
What you do
rows: Dehydrated skin

Skin that lacks **water** (not oil). Any type can be dehydrated, even oily skin. It feels tight, looks dull and has fine, crepey surface lines. Caused by sun, air conditioning, harsh products and too little water to drink.
Hydrating products; stop harsh, alcohol-based products; advise drinking water.
Comedones
Blocked pores. Open comedones are **blackheads** (the oil darkens in the air); closed ones are whiteheads.
Deep cleanse, steam, gentle extraction if suitable; clay mask.
Milia
Small, hard, white bumps of trapped skin cells, often around the eyes and cheeks.
Do not squeeze: they have no opening. Removal needs a sterile lancet and further training or a doctor.
Open (enlarged) pores
Visible pores, mostly on the nose and cheeks of oily skin.
Deep cleanse; clay mask; astringent on oily areas.
Spots and pustules
Raised red spots, some with pus.
Avoid them: never squeeze. Severe, painful acne needs a doctor.
Hyperpigmentation
Patches darker than the skin around them: from sun, hormones, or healing after spots, cuts or rough squeezing. Very common on deeper skin tones.
Gentle care, no picking or harsh scrubs, daily sunscreen. Fading takes months; refer to a doctor for patches that worry her.
Hypopigmentation
Patches lighter than the surrounding skin.
Protect from the sun; refer to a doctor if new or spreading.
Broken capillaries
Tiny red veins on the cheeks and nose; common in sensitive skin.
No strong heat, no tapotement, no hot towels on them; light pressure.
Small dark raised spots on the cheeks
Common, harmless spots on many deeper skin tones.
Leave them alone; do not try to remove them. A doctor can advise.
Keloid scars
Raised, thick scars that grow beyond the injury; more common on deeper skin tones.
Avoid any injury to the skin: no squeezing or harsh exfoliation.
Razor bumps (ingrown hairs)
Red bumps in the beard area where shaved hairs curl back into the skin.
Gentle products; no hard scrubbing; never pick them.

blocks.note: **Dry and dehydrated are not the same.** Dry skin lacks oil; dehydrated skin lacks water. An oily skin that feels tight after harsh, drying products is dehydrated, and stripping it further makes it worse.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Deeper skin tones mark easily: rough squeezing, harsh scrubs, picking or a burn can leave dark patches that take months to fade. Gentle hands and daily sun protection matter for every client in Jamaica's strong sun.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: The consultation tells you whether the facial is safe, what the client wants, and how to plan it. Do it in private, explain each step, fill in the record card together, and have the client sign it before you start.

head: Ask about
Why it matters
rows: What she wants from the facial
Lets you plan the products and the treatment and keep her expectations realistic.
Medical history and medicines (for example high blood pressure, diabetes, heart problems, epilepsy, pregnancy)
Some need less heat, a gentler treatment or her doctor's advice first. Record them; never ignore them.
Skin medicines and creams (for example retinoid creams or acne tablets)
They make the skin thin and easily irritated: no exfoliation or strong products.
Allergies (nuts, fragrance, lanolin, plasters) and past reactions
So you avoid ingredients that could cause a reaction. Read the labels.
Her skin-care routine and the products she uses at home
Shows how her skin is cared for and which products may be causing problems; guides your home-care advice.
Recent treatments (peels, waxing or threading of the face, laser, injections)
Recently treated skin is sensitive; some areas must be avoided for a time.
Lifestyle: sun, water intake, sleep, smoking, stress
All show in the skin and shape your advice.
Contact lenses
Take them out before steam and masks.

blocks.p: A contraindication that **prevents** the facial means it must not go ahead. One that **restricts** the facial means you adapt it, or avoid an area.

head: Prevents the facial (refer to a doctor)
Restricts the facial (adapt it)
rows: Bacterial infections: impetigo (weeping sores with honey-coloured crusts), boils
Viral infections: cold sores (herpes simplex)
Fungal infections: ringworm (tinea), a red, ring-shaped scaly patch
Eye infections such as conjunctivitis
A severe skin condition that has flared up, or broken, weeping skin
Fever or feeling unwell
Recent surgery or injury to the face
A small cut or graze: avoid it
A bruise: avoid it
A few spots: work around them
Broken capillaries: less heat, light pressure
Mild, unbroken eczema or psoriasis: gentle, fragrance-free products
Recent sunburn on one area: avoid it
High or low blood pressure: less heat, sit up slowly
Diabetes: gentle handling, slow healing
Allergies: avoid the ingredient
Pregnancy: gentle products; check the makers' advice

blocks.note: You are not a doctor. Do not name a disease. Explain kindly and privately that the facial cannot be done today (or must be changed), advise her to see a doctor or pharmacist, record what you saw, and offer to rebook when she is well.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Infections such as cold sores and impetigo pass by touch: from her skin to your hands, sponges and products, and on to the next client or to her own eyes. After any contagious condition, bin single-use items, clean and disinfect everything she touched, and wash your hands.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: A first facial just before a big event (a wedding, a photo shoot) is risky: the skin may redden, react or break out. Advise clients to book at least a week before.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Ask her to remove jewellery and keep it safe
Ask her to remove upper clothing as needed and lie on the couch
Cover her with a towel for warmth and modesty
Put on a clean headband or turban to keep the hair off the face
Contact lenses out
Wash your hands

blocks.p: The superficial (first) cleanse removes make-up and surface dirt. Work in this order, with light, careful movements, keeping products out of the eyes.

flow: Eyes: hold a cotton pad soaked in eye make-up remover on the closed eye for a few seconds to loosen mascara
Under the eye, wipe gently from the outer corner towards the inner corner; on the lid, wipe down the lashes
Lips: support one corner and wipe across
Face and neck: apply cleanser with light upward strokes
Remove it with damp cotton pads or sponges, working upward

blocks.p: Analyse the skin **after the superficial cleanse**, because make-up hides its true condition. Cover the eyes with damp cotton pads, bring the magnifying lamp over, and look closely at each area. Feel the skin too, for texture, firmness and oiliness.

head: Check
What you look for
rows: Skin type
Normal, dry, oily, combination, sensitive or mature.
T-zone and cheeks
Shine, open pores and blackheads on the forehead, nose and chin; dryness or flaking on the cheeks.
Texture and tone
Smooth or rough; even colour or dark and light patches.
Conditions
Comedones, milia, spots, dehydration, broken capillaries, pigmentation, scars.
Firmness
Elasticity and lines; signs of ageing.
Contraindications
Anything you missed at the consultation.

blocks.p: Record your findings on the skin analysis chart, explain them to the client in simple words, and agree the products for the rest of the facial.

ul: Apply cleanser again to the face and neck, and work it into the skin with small circles and upward movements for a few minutes, paying attention to the T-zone.
Remove every trace with damp pads, sponges or mitts. Cleanser left on the skin blocks pores and stops later products working.

head: Cleanser
Suits
rows: Foaming gel or wash
Oily and combination skin; men's skin.
Cleansing lotion (milk)
Normal, combination and young skin.
Cleansing cream or balm
Dry and mature skin; removing heavy make-up.
Mild, fragrance-free cleanser
Sensitive skin.

blocks.p: Toner removes the last traces of cleanser, refreshes the skin and helps it feel balanced. Apply it on damp cotton pads with light strokes, or mist it on, then blot with a tissue.

head: Type
Strength
Suits
rows: Freshener (skin tonic)
Mildest; usually alcohol-free
Dry, sensitive and mature skin.
Toner
Medium
Normal and combination skin.
Astringent
Strongest; often contains alcohol; tightens and removes oil
Oily skin and oily areas only.

blocks.note: An alcohol-based astringent used all over a combination or dry skin strips the cheeks and can leave them tight and dehydrated. Match the toner to each area.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Exfoliation** removes dead skin cells from the surface. The skin looks brighter and smoother, and later products work better.

head: Type
How it works
Suits
Take care
rows: Scrub (mechanical)
Fine grains rubbed gently over the skin.
Normal, oily and combination skin.
Gentle pressure; avoid the eyes, cuts and spots. No coarse, sharp grains on the face.
Enzyme exfoliant
Fruit enzymes (for example from papaya or pineapple) dissolve dead cells without rubbing.
Sensitive, dry and mature skin; skin with spots.
Leave on for the maker's time; keep warm and moist if the maker says.
Mild acid exfoliant
Gentle acids loosen dead cells.
As the maker and your training allow.
Not on sensitive skin or skin on retinoids.

ul: Do not exfoliate broken skin, active spots, sunburn, or an area that was waxed or threaded recently.
No exfoliation for clients using retinoid creams or acne tablets: the skin is already thin.
At home, most skins need exfoliating only once or twice a week.

blocks.note: Home-made scrubs with lime or lemon juice are a bad idea. Citrus juice on the skin in strong sun can cause burns and dark patches, and sugar crystals are too rough for facial skin.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Steam warms and softens the skin, increases the blood flow, and helps loosen blocked pores before extraction or a mask.

flow: Check the cable; fill with distilled water to the line
Switch on with the nozzle turned away from the client
Wait until the steam flows steadily, with no spitting
Cover her eyes with damp cotton pads
Turn the steam towards her at the planned distance
Time it and stay with her throughout
Turn it away and switch off

head: Skin
Typical plan (follow the maker and your instructor)
rows: Oily, congested, normal
About 30 to 40 cm from the face for about 5 to 10 minutes.
Dry or mature
Further away and shorter.
Sensitive, broken capillaries, high blood pressure
Further away and only a few minutes, or no steam: use a **warm (not hot) compress**, tested on your wrist, instead.
Clients with breathing problems who find steam uncomfortable
Leave it out; use a warm compress.

blocks.note: Too close or too long, steam can scald, irritate and redden the skin and dry it out. Never leave a client alone under steam.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Some facials include removing blackheads (extraction). Only do it after steam, when the pores are soft, and only if your Centre allows it.

ul: Wear gloves. Wrap your fingertips in tissue or damp cotton.
Press gently down and inwards on each side of the blackhead. If it does not come out with light pressure, leave it.
Keep it short: a few minutes in total.
**Never** squeeze red, swollen, infected spots or milia, and never use your nails or a pin.
Afterwards, wipe with a soothing antiseptic or astringent toner.

blocks.note: Heavy squeezing bruises the skin, breaks capillaries, spreads infection and can leave scars and dark marks, especially on deeper skin tones.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Massage relaxes the client, warms the skin, increases the blood flow, helps remove dead cells and waste, and tones the muscles. A facial massage usually lasts about 10 to 15 minutes. Use a massage cream (normal and dry skin), an oil (dry skin) or a light lotion or gel (oily skin).

head: Movement
How you do it
Effect
Use it
rows: Effleurage
Smooth, gliding strokes with the palms or finger pads, even pressure.
Relaxes, warms the skin, spreads the medium.
To begin and end the massage and to link the other movements.
Petrissage
Kneading: lifting, squeezing, rolling or gently pinching the muscles.
Improves blood flow and muscle tone; stimulates.
On the cheeks, jaw and neck of normal and oily skin; lighter on dry skin.
Tapotement (tapping)
Light, quick tapping with the fingertips.
Stimulates and tones.
Only on firm, healthy skin. Leave it out for sensitive skin and broken capillaries.
Vibration
A fine, fast trembling of the fingertips or hands, held on one spot.
Soothes the nerves; can also stimulate.
Over the forehead or along nerves, briefly.
Frictions
Small, firm circles with the finger pads, moving the skin over the tissue beneath.
Loosens tight areas; helps shed dead cells.
Around the chin, nose and forehead.

ul: Work **upward and outward**, following the muscles and lifting, never dragging the skin down.
Keep an even pressure and a steady rhythm, and keep one hand in contact with the face so the client is not startled.
Light pressure on the delicate skin around the eyes.
Ask about pressure and comfort, and watch her face for signs of discomfort.

blocks.h: When to change or leave out the massage

head: Situation
What to do
rows: Sensitive skin; broken capillaries
Light effleurage and gentle movements; no tapotement; less time.
Active spots or acne
Avoid the area; massage can spread infection and inflame the spots.
Swelling, bruising, recent injury or sunburn
Avoid the area.
Recent cosmetic injections or face surgery
No massage on the area until the doctor says it is safe.
High blood pressure
Slow, relaxing movements; no vigorous stimulating work.
Client unwell or uncomfortable
Stop or shorten the massage.

sections.title: Masks, moisturising and adapting the facial

head: Mask
What it does
Suits
rows: Setting mask (for example a clay mask)
Dries and tightens on the skin; absorbs oil, deep-cleans the pores and stimulates.
Oily and combination skin (the T-zone); normal skin in a thin layer.
Non-setting mask (cream, gel or sheet mask)
Stays soft and moist; soothes, hydrates and calms.
Dry, dehydrated, sensitive and mature skin.

blocks.note: Combination skin can have two masks at once: clay on the oily T-zone and a cream or gel mask on the cheeks.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Take the mask out of the jar with a clean spatula into a clean bowl
Place damp cotton pads over the eyes
Apply an even layer with a clean mask brush, working from the neck upward
Keep it off the eyes, eyebrows, lips, nostrils and hairline
Leave it for the maker's time and stay with the client
Soften it with warm, damp sponges or mitts and wipe it away gently, working upward
Tone the skin

blocks.note: Never let the client peel off a dried clay mask, and do not rub it off dry: soften it with warm water first. If the skin stings, itches or swells under a mask, remove it at once with cool water.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Skin
Moisturiser
rows: Oily or combination
Light, oil-free lotion or gel labelled **non-comedogenic** (unlikely to block pores).
Dry or mature
A richer cream.
Sensitive
Fragrance-free, mild.
All skins, by day
A moisturiser or sunscreen with broad-spectrum **SPF** (sun protection factor).

blocks.p: Apply it with light, upward effleurage strokes over the face and neck and blot any excess with a tissue. A small amount of eye cream may be patted around the eyes, and a lip balm applied.

blocks.note: Fresh, newly cleansed and exfoliated skin burns more easily. Jamaica's sun is strong all year, so every daytime facial finishes with sun protection.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Skin
Cleanser and toner
Exfoliate and steam
Massage
Mask
rows: Oily
Foaming gel; astringent
Scrub or enzyme; steam about 10 minutes
Full massage, lighter on spots
Clay
Dry
Cream; freshener
Enzyme; short steam, further away
Rich cream, gentle petrissage
Cream or gel
Combination
Lotion; astringent on T-zone, freshener on cheeks
Scrub on T-zone, gentle elsewhere; steam
Full massage
Clay on T-zone, cream on cheeks
Sensitive
Mild, fragrance-free; freshener
Mild enzyme or none; warm compress instead of steam
Light, short, no tapotement
Soothing cream or gel

ul: Men's skin is often thicker and oilier, and the beard area is sensitive from daily shaving.
Advise him to shave the day before, not just before, the facial: freshly shaved skin stings with products.
Work gently over the beard area, with the hair growth in mind: remove products with damp pads or hot towels rather than sponges that catch on stubble.
Keep setting masks out of a beard: clay dries in the hair, pulls and is hard to remove.
Razor bumps: gentle products, no hard scrubbing, no picking. Home care: shave in the direction of growth with a sharp blade, and do not stretch the skin.

blocks.note: A full facial usually takes about an hour from start to finish. Plan the time for each stage so the massage and mask are not rushed.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **contra-action** is an unwanted reaction during or after a treatment. Know what is normal, what is not, and what to do.

head: Contra-action
What you see
What you do
rows: Mild redness (erythema)
Pinkness after massage, steam or exfoliation; fades within a short time.
Normal: more blood is flowing to the skin. Reassure her.
Allergic reaction or irritation
Strong redness, itching, burning, swelling, a rash or bumps.
Stop; remove the product at once with cool water; apply a cool compress. If it does not settle, advise a doctor. Record the product.
Product in the eye
Stinging, watering, red eye.
Rinse at once with plenty of clean, cool water or sterile eye wash; get medical help if it stays sore.
Faint or dizzy
Pale, light-headed, sick; often from heat or sitting up too fast.
Stop; turn off the steam; let her lie, then sit up slowly; give water; let her rest.
Burn from steam or a hot towel
Red, painful skin; perhaps blisters.
Cool under cool running water (about 20 minutes); no creams; get first aid help; record it.
Breakouts in the days after
New spots as the skin is deep-cleaned.
Advise her not to pick; review products at the next visit.
Bruising or broken capillaries
After heavy extraction or pressure.
Prevent: gentle pressure only; avoid sensitive areas.

blocks.note: Record every contra-action on the record card and tell your supervisor. If a reaction was to a product, write the product's name so it is never used on her again.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Remove the headband; help her sit up slowly and let her sit for a moment before she stands.
Offer a glass of water and a mirror; explain what you did and what you found.

head: Advice
Why
rows: No make-up for the rest of the day, if she can
The pores are clean and open; make-up can block them.
Avoid strong sun, sea bathing in the heat of the day, saunas and steam rooms for about a day
The skin is warm and freshly exfoliated, so it reddens and burns more easily.
Do not touch, pick or squeeze
Hands spread germs; picking scars and marks the skin.
Tell the salon about any lasting redness, itching or spots
So a reaction can be dealt with and recorded.

ul: Cleanse, tone and moisturise **morning and night**, with products for her skin type.
Use a broad-spectrum sunscreen every day, even when it is cloudy: Jamaica's sun ages the skin and darkens patches.
Exfoliate gently once or twice a week; use a suitable mask about once a week.
Drink plenty of water; sleep and a balanced diet help the skin.
Book the next facial in about four weeks.

blocks.p: Recommend products that suit her skin type and needs, explain how to use them, give the price in J$, and let her decide. Never promise that a product will cure a skin problem.

head: What to record
Example
rows: Date, client's details, signature
07/11/2026, Paulette Wright, Bog Walk; signed
Medical details and contraindications
High blood pressure (medicine); no contraindications seen
Skin analysis
Combination; open pores and blackheads on nose; dehydrated cheeks
Products, steam and massage
Lotion cleanser; enzyme exfoliant; steam 40 cm, 5 minutes (reduced for blood pressure); 12-minute massage, no tapotement; clay on T-zone, cream mask on cheeks; SPF 30 moisturiser
Reactions
Mild redness after massage, settled before she left
Advice and products bought
Home-care plan given in writing; alcohol-free toner, J$ 2,800
Therapist
Trainee's name, checked by the instructor

blocks.note: Record cards are personal information. Under Jamaica's Data Protection Act keep them private and secure, and never discuss a client's skin with other clients.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Bin single-use items in the lined, lidded bin
Towels and headband into the laundry bin
Wash and disinfect bowls and brushes
Empty, clean and dry the steamer as the maker says
Cover the magnifying lamp
Wipe the couch and trolley with disinfectant; fresh couch roll
Close and wipe the products; wash your hands

ul: I can prepare a clean, warm, private room, couch and trolley, and keep the facial hygienic.
I can check and use a steamer, a magnifying lamp and hot towels safely.
I can describe the epidermis, dermis and subcutaneous layer, and what the sebaceous glands do.
I can recognise normal, dry, oily, combination, sensitive and mature skin.
I can tell dry skin from dehydrated skin, and recognise comedones, milia, hyperpigmentation and broken capillaries.
I can carry out a consultation and say why each question matters.
I can name contraindications that prevent a facial and ones that restrict it, and refer a client kindly.
I can carry out a superficial cleanse, a skin analysis under the lamp and a deep cleanse.
I can choose a cleanser, toner, exfoliant, mask and moisturiser for each skin type.
I can steam the skin safely and replace steam with a warm compress for sensitive skin.
I can explain when extraction is safe and how to do it gently.
I can use the five massage movements upward and outward, and adapt or leave out the massage.
I can apply and remove setting and non-setting masks correctly.
I can adapt a facial for a male client and for deeper skin tones.
I can deal with contra-actions, give aftercare and home-care advice, and complete the records.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. For example: 'I pre-heat the steamer with the nozzle turned away from the client, so that any spitting water cannot scald her.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: The outer layer of the skin.
The layer under the epidermis, with collagen, elastin, blood vessels, nerves and glands.
Glands in the dermis that make sebum, the skin's natural oil.
The pigment that gives skin its colour.
The slightly acid film of sweat and sebum that protects the skin.
The forehead, nose and chin; often the oiliest area.
An oily T-zone with normal or dry cheeks.
Skin that reddens and reacts easily.
Small, hard, white bumps of trapped skin cells.
Patches darker than the surrounding skin.
Tiny visible red veins, usually on the cheeks and nose.
Something that prevents a treatment or means it must be changed.
An unwanted reaction during or after a treatment.
Redness of the skin caused by more blood flowing to it.
The virus that causes cold sores.
A contagious bacterial skin infection with weeping, crusted sores.
The first cleanse, removing make-up and surface dirt.
The second, longer cleanse that works the cleanser into the skin.
A lit magnifying lens for close skin analysis.
A strong toner, often with alcohol, for oily skin.
Removing dead skin cells from the surface.
An exfoliant that dissolves dead cells without rubbing.
Water with the minerals removed; used in steamers.
Smooth, gliding strokes that begin, link and end a massage.
Kneading movements that lift, squeeze and roll the muscles.
Light, quick tapping with the fingertips.
Small, firm circular movements with the finger pads.
A mask that dries and tightens on the skin, such as clay.
A mask that stays soft and moist, such as cream or gel.
Made so that it is unlikely to block pores.
Sun protection factor: how well a product protects against sunburn.
Disposable paper roll that covers the couch for each client.
A rigid container for used lancets and blades.
The form on which you record skin type and conditions.

c1.title: An accountant's skin in New Kingston
c1.text: Renée Lindo, 29, is an accountant in New Kingston who wears foundation every day and sits in air conditioning. Under the magnifying lamp, trainee Gillian sees shine, open pores and blackheads across the forehead, nose and chin, while the cheeks are smooth, slightly flaky and feel tight. Renée says she wipes an alcohol-based astringent over her whole face morning and night 'to stop the oil'.

c2.title: A tour rep with easily flushed skin in Ocho Rios
c2.text: Mrs. Patricia Henry, 47, works outdoors as a tour representative in Ocho Rios. Her fair skin flushes red quickly, there are tiny red veins on her cheeks and nose, and she says a perfumed cream once made her face sting and itch. She washes her face with very hot water and scrubs it with a rough cloth every evening. She wants a relaxing facial.

c3.title: Two days before a wedding in Savanna-la-Mar
c3.text: Kerine Ellis, 31, books her first ever facial for two days before her wedding in Savanna-la-Mar. At the consultation, trainee Andrea sees a small cluster of blisters at the corner of Kerine's top lip, some starting to crust. Kerine says it tingled yesterday and that she 'gets them now and then when stressed'.

c4.title: Steamer trouble in the May Pen training salon
c4.text: In the Centre's training salon in May Pen, trainee Rushelle fills the steamer from the tap because the distilled water has run out. She switches it on and turns it straight towards her client, and it spits drops of water. Her written plan says: 'Steam 10 cm from the face for 20 minutes.' The sponges she used on her last client are rinsed under the tap, ready to use again.

c5.title: A security guard's facial in Montego Bay
c5.text: Mr. Dwayne Barrett, 38, a security guard in Montego Bay, has his first facial. He has a full, short beard, an oily T-zone with blackheads, and dark marks on his cheeks where he squeezed spots in the past. He shaved his neck just before he came, and asks whether the facial will 'get rid of the dark marks today'.

questions.q: Which skin type do Gillian's findings point to for Renée?
o: Oily
Combination
Sensitive
Normal
questions.why: An oily T-zone (forehead, nose and chin) with normal or dry cheeks is combination skin, the most common type. Each area is treated for what it needs.

questions.q: Which mask plan suits Renée's skin best?
o: A clay mask all over, left until it cracks
A rich cream mask all over, for the flakes
Clay on the T-zone and a cream mask on the cheeks
No mask, as combination skin cannot have one
questions.why: A setting clay mask absorbs oil and clears the pores of the T-zone, while a non-setting cream or gel mask hydrates and soothes the tight, flaky cheeks. One mask all over would suit only half her face.

questions.q: What should Gillian advise about Renée's astringent?
o: Use it more often, as the cheeks need their oil removed too, morning and night
Keep any astringent to the T-zone; use an alcohol-free toner elsewhere
Stop all toners and wash the whole face with bar soap and hot water instead
Swap it for a body oil, so the whole face stays moist
questions.why: An alcohol-based astringent all over strips the drier cheeks, leaving them tight and dehydrated. Match the toner to each area: a mild, alcohol-free toner for the cheeks, and a stronger one only on oily areas if needed.

questions.q: Renée asks Gillian to remove the blackheads on her nose. How should this be done?
o: Before the cleanse, while the skin is still cool and firm, with bare fingers
With the nails, pressing hard until each one comes out
After steam, with gloved, tissue-wrapped fingers and light pressure
With a pin to open each pore first, including any red spots, then a clay mask
questions.why: Steam softens the pores first. Gloves and tissue protect both of you, and light pressure avoids bruising and marks; a blackhead that will not come out easily is left alone, and red or infected spots are never squeezed.

questions.q: How should Gillian's colleague change the steam for Mrs. Henry?
o: Use a warm, wrist-tested compress, or brief steam far away
Steam her closer and longer, to open her pores deeply
Add a few drops of lime juice to the steamer water
Use a hot towel pressed firmly over her cheeks
questions.why: Heat makes sensitive skin and broken capillaries redder. Use a warm (not hot) compress tested on the wrist, or only a little steam well away from the face. Lime juice and very hot towels would irritate her skin.

questions.q: Which moisturiser should finish Mrs. Henry's facial?
o: A rich, perfumed night cream to calm the redness
An alcohol-based gel that cools and tightens the skin
A thick body lotion, which protects better outdoors
A fragrance-free moisturiser with broad-spectrum SPF
questions.why: Fragrance has already made her skin react, so choose fragrance-free products. She works outdoors in strong sun after a facial, so broad-spectrum sun protection is essential.

questions.q: What home-care advice will help Mrs. Henry's red veins most?
o: Rub ice straight onto the cheeks every night to shrink the tiny veins
Use lukewarm water and a gentle cleanser, with no rough cloth
Use a strong astringent to shrink the tiny veins
Scrub twice a day with the rough cloth to remove the redness from the surface
questions.why: Very hot water, rough scrubbing and extremes of heat or cold make broken capillaries worse. Lukewarm water and gentle, fragrance-free products protect sensitive skin.

questions.q: What should Andrea do about the blisters on Kerine's lip?
o: Give the full facial, but keep the mask and massage off the lip area
Steam the area for longer to dry the blisters out
Explain the facial cannot go ahead and suggest a pharmacist
Cover the blisters with concealer and carry on with the full facial
questions.why: Blisters that tingle and crust at the lip are likely a cold sore (herpes simplex), which is contagious and prevents a facial. Explain kindly without naming a disease, suggest a pharmacist or doctor, and rebook when it has healed.

questions.q: Why does a cold sore stop the whole facial, not just work near the lip?
o: It is a virus that hands, sponges and products can spread
The massage cream would make the sore spread to the scalp
It only shows that her skin type is dry and very sensitive
Cold sores are caused by facial steam, so it must be avoided
questions.why: The virus passes by touch. Your hands, sponges and products would carry it across her face (even to her eyes) and to the next client, so the facial waits until the sore has healed.

questions.q: Kerine wants to rebook for the day before her wedding. What is the best advice?
o: The day before is best, so the glow is at its peak
Have it the morning of the wedding, with extra steam
Any day is fine, as a first facial never causes a reaction
Book a first facial a week or more before a big event
questions.why: A first facial can leave redness, a reaction or a few spots while the skin settles. Booking at least a week before gives time for that, and for the cold sore to heal.

questions.q: The steamer spits drops of water at the client. What should Rushelle do first?
o: Carry on, as the spitting stops once it warms up
Turn it away from the client and switch it off
Cover the client's face with a dry towel and carry on
Top up the tank while it is still switched on
questions.why: Hot drops can scald. Turn the nozzle away from the client and switch off, then check the water. A steamer is always pre-heated facing away until the steam is steady, and never filled while switched on.

questions.q: Why do steamer makers usually ask for distilled water rather than tap water?
o: Tap water makes the steam too cool to open the pores
Distilled water has a scent that relaxes the client
Tap water leaves mineral scale, which can cause spitting
Distilled water gives off ozone that kills skin germs
questions.why: Hard tap water leaves mineral scale on the heater, which can make the steamer spit and work badly. Distilled water has the minerals removed. Follow the maker's instructions and descale as they say.

questions.q: What is wrong with Rushelle's plan to steam 10 cm from the face for 20 minutes?
o: Nothing: closer and longer steam always cleans the pores much better
It is far too close and too long, risking burns and irritation
The distance is fine, but 20 minutes is far too short to open the pores
Steam must always touch the skin, so 10 cm is too far
questions.why: Steam is usually given about 30 to 40 cm away for about 5 to 10 minutes on normal or oily skin, and less on dry or sensitive skin. Too close and too long can scald, redden and dry the skin.

questions.q: What should happen to the sponges Rushelle used on her last client?
o: Rinse them well under the tap and use them again on the next client
Dry them in the sun, which kills all the germs
Keep them in a bag for the same client's next facial
Bin disposable ones; wash and disinfect reusable ones
questions.why: Sponges hold germs and product. Disposable sponges go in the lined, lidded bin; reusable ones are washed and disinfected (or laundered) as the maker says before another client. Rinsing or sun-drying is not enough.

questions.q: Where should the clay mask go on Mr. Barrett's face?
o: On the T-zone and cheeks above the beard, not in the beard
All over, including the beard, to clean the hair too
Only on the beard, where the most oil is trapped
On the lips and around the eyes, where the skin is oily
questions.why: Clay dries in beard hair, pulls as it sets and is hard to remove, so keep it to the oily skin above the beard line. Masks never go on the eyes or lips.

questions.q: How should the trainee answer Mr. Barrett's question about his dark marks?
o: Yes: one deep facial with a strong scrub will lift the marks off the surface
Yes: a skin-bleaching cream applied after the facial will clear them within days
No: they are marks from old spots; sunscreen and no squeezing help them fade
No: dark marks on deeper skin tones are permanent, so no product or care helps them
questions.why: Dark marks after spots are hyperpigmentation. They fade slowly, over months, with daily sun protection, gentle care and no squeezing; harsh scrubs and bleaching products can make them worse. Be honest and never promise a quick cure.

questions.q: What should Mr. Barrett do about shaving before his next facial?
o: Shave just before he arrives so the products reach the skin
Never shave again, as shaving causes every skin problem
Shave against the growth that morning for a closer finish
Shave the day before, so the skin is not raw for the facial
questions.why: Freshly shaved skin is tender, and products and exfoliants sting it. Shaving the day before gives the skin time to settle. Shaving against the growth makes razor bumps more likely.

questions.q: Which layer of the skin holds the collagen and elastin fibres, the blood vessels and the sebaceous glands?
o: The subcutaneous layer
The epidermis
The acid mantle
The dermis
questions.why: The dermis lies under the epidermis and holds the fibres that keep skin firm and stretchy, plus blood vessels, nerves, hair follicles and glands. The subcutaneous layer below it is mostly fat.

questions.q: A therapist rests her fingertips on the client's forehead and makes a fine, fast trembling movement. Which movement is this?
o: Vibration
Tapotement
Frictions
Effleurage
questions.why: Vibration is a fine, rapid trembling held in one place, which soothes the nerves. Tapotement is light tapping, frictions are small firm circles, and effleurage is smooth gliding strokes.

questions.q: A client asks you to squeeze out the small, hard white bumps under her eyes. What should you do?
o: Squeeze them firmly with tissue-wrapped fingers after steam
Scrub over them hard each visit until they wear away
Explain they are milia, which cannot be squeezed out safely
Prick each one open with a clean pin from your kit
questions.why: Milia are trapped skin cells under the surface with no opening, so squeezing only bruises and marks the skin. Removing them needs a sterile lancet and further training, or a doctor.
